meta.disclaimer: VoiceHealth provides general health and wellness information only. It does not diagnose medical conditions or prescribe medication, and always encourages users to consult a qualified healthcare professional. Note: This knowledge base includes MSTG entries (M001-M070), gym/fitness musculoskeletal entries, and common condition entries. For rule-based search with synonyms and pattern matching, refer to assets/keyword_rules.json and the KnowledgeBase class in lib/services/knowledge_base_service.dart
meta.note: Updated knowledge base. Contains 24 original entries + 70 MSTG entries (M001-M070) + 50 gym/fitness/musculoskeletal entries. New entries have collision-free IDs. For full rule-based search, see keyword_rules.json

entries.content: Most adults need about 7 to 9 hours of sleep a night. A regular sleep routine and a calm, dark, quiet bedroom help you fall asleep and wake up refreshed.
tips: Go to bed and wake up at about the same time every day
Avoid caffeine, heavy meals and phone screens close to bedtime
Keep your bedroom cool, dark and quiet
entries.see_doctor_if: You have trouble sleeping for several weeks, snore loudly with pauses in breathing, or feel so sleepy in the day that it affects your work or safety.
entries.source: NHS - How to get to sleep

entries.content: Regular physical activity helps protect the heart, control weight, strengthen bones and improve mood. Adults are generally advised to aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate activity a week, such as brisk walking, and children about 60 minutes a day.
tips: Start slowly and build up gradually
Break activity into short sessions, for example 10 minutes at a time
Choose activities you enjoy so you keep doing them
entries.see_doctor_if: You get chest pain, severe breathlessness or dizziness when active. Check with a health worker before starting if you are older, very inactive, or have a heart condition.

entries.content: Everyone feels stress sometimes. Talking to someone you trust, slow breathing, regular activity and enough sleep can help you cope. Breaking big problems into small steps also makes them easier to handle.
tips: Talk to a friend, family member or faith leader you trust
Try slow breathing: in for four counts, out for six
Limit alcohol and keep to regular sleep and meals
entries.see_doctor_if: Stress or low mood lasts more than two weeks or affects daily life. If you have thoughts of harming yourself, seek help right away from a health worker, a trusted person, or emergency services.
entries.source: WHO - Doing What Matters in Times of Stress

entries.content: Your body needs fluids to work well. Many health services suggest around 6 to 8 glasses of fluid a day, and more in hot weather, during exercise or when you are ill. Clean water is the best choice, and pale yellow urine is a rough sign you are drinking enough.
tips: Sip water regularly through the day
Choose water over sugary drinks
Drink more in hot weather or when active
entries.see_doctor_if: You have extreme thirst, very dark urine, dizziness or very little urine. If you have a kidney or heart condition, follow the fluid advice your health worker gave you.

entries.content: A healthy diet includes a variety of foods: vegetables, fruits, whole grains, beans, nuts and some animal-source foods. Aim for at least five portions of fruit and vegetables a day, and go easy on sugary drinks, fried food and processed snacks.
tips: Fill half your plate with vegetables and fruit
Choose beans, groundnuts, fish or eggs as protein
Cut back on sugary drinks and fried foods
entries.see_doctor_if: You have unexplained weight loss or gain, constant tiredness, or you follow a very restricted diet. A health worker or dietitian can give personal advice.

keywords: what to eat for high blood pressure
entries.content: Eating less salt can help keep blood pressure in a healthy range. WHO advises adults to have less than 5 grams of salt a day, about one teaspoon. Fruit, vegetables and fresh, unprocessed foods also support healthy blood pressure.
tips: Cook with less salt and fewer stock cubes
Limit salty snacks, processed meats and salty sauces
Eat more fruit, vegetables and beans
entries.see_doctor_if: You get severe headache, chest pain, blurred vision or confusion. Seek urgent care. Also have your blood pressure checked regularly.
entries.source: WHO - Hypertension fact sheet; WHO - Salt reduction fact sheet

entries.content: Healthy eating helps manage blood sugar. Choose whole grains, beans, vegetables and lean protein, eat at regular times, watch portion sizes, and limit sugary drinks and sweets.
tips: Replace sugary drinks with water
Eat regular meals and avoid long gaps
Ask a health worker or dietitian for a personal meal plan
entries.see_doctor_if: You have very high thirst, frequent urination, unexplained weight loss, or your blood sugar swings a lot. Seek urgent care for vomiting, fainting or vomiting.
entries.source: WHO - Diabetes fact sheet; NHS - Eating well with diabetes

entries.content: WHO advises feeding babies only breast milk for the first 6 months. From 6 months, add safe, nutritious foods such as enriched porridge, mashed beans, eggs, fruit and vegetables, while continuing to breastfeed up to 2 years or beyond.
tips: Start solid foods at 6 months, not earlier
Offer a variety of foods and increase amounts as the child grows
Wash hands and use clean utensils when preparing baby food
entries.see_doctor_if: Your child is not gaining weight, looks very thin, has swollen feet or face, seems very tired, or refuses to feed. Take them to a health facility for a growth check.
entries.source: WHO - Infant and young child feeding fact sheet

entries.content: Washing hands with soap and clean water is one of the simplest ways to prevent diarrhoea, colds, flu and many other infections. Scrub for at least 20 seconds, covering palms, backs of hands, between fingers and under nails.
tips: Wash before eating or preparing food
Wash after using the toilet or changing a nappy
Wash after coughing, sneezing or caring for someone who is sick
entries.see_doctor_if: You develop diarrhoea, vomiting or fever despite good hygiene, or your skin stays cracked or sore from washing.
entries.source: WHO - Hand hygiene guidance; NHS - How to wash your hands

entries.content: Malaria is spread by mosquito bites. Sleeping under an insecticide-treated net every night is one of the best protections. Removing standing water near your home reduces mosquito breeding.
tips: Sleep under a treated mosquito net every night
Empty or cover containers holding stagnant water
Wear long sleeves in the evening and use repellent if available
entries.see_doctor_if: You have fever, chills or flu-like symptoms, even if you use prevention. Go for a malaria test promptly. Pregnant women should follow the malaria prevention advice from their antenatal clinic.

entries.content: Unsafe water can spread diarrhoeal diseases such as cholera. Boil drinking water to a rolling boil, or treat it with chlorine as advised by local health services, and store it in a clean, covered container.
tips: Boil or treat water if you are unsure it is safe
Keep stored water covered and use a clean cup to pour
Wash hands before handling water and food
entries.see_doctor_if: You have severe watery diarrhoea or repeated vomiting. Go to a health facility immediately and sip oral rehydration solution on the way.
entries.source: WHO - Drinking-water fact sheet; WHO - Cholera fact sheet

entries.content: Vaccines protect against serious diseases such as measles, polio and tetanus. Children should follow the national immunization schedule at a health facility, and you should keep their child health card and bring it to every visit.
tips: Keep the child health card safe and bring it to each visit
Ask your clinic which vaccines are due
Ask about vaccines for adults and pregnant women too
entries.see_doctor_if: You have missed vaccines, so visit your nearest health facility. Seek care if a child has a high fever, a seizure, severe swelling or constant crying after a vaccine.
entries.source: WHO - Immunization fact sheet; Ministry of Health immunization schedule

entries.content: Paracetamol is commonly used to relieve mild to moderate pain and to bring down fever. Always follow the label or a health worker's advice, because taking more than recommended can seriously damage the liver. Check other cold and flu products, as many also contain paracetamol.
tips: Follow the instructions on the packet or from a pharmacist
Do not combine it with other products containing paracetamol
Keep medicines out of children's reach
entries.see_doctor_if: Pain or fever lasts more than a few days, fever is very high, or you think you took too much. Seek urgent medical help for a suspected overdose.
entries.source: NHS - Paracetamol for adults; MedlinePlus - Acetaminophen

entries.content: Ibuprofen is a type of medicine called an NSAID, commonly used for pain, inflammation and fever. It can irritate the stomach, so it is usually best taken with or after food. It is not suitable for everyone.
tips: Take with or after food
Ask a pharmacist first if you have asthma, kidney, heart or stomach problems
Do not use if you are pregnant unless a health worker advises it
entries.see_doctor_if: You get black stools, vomit blood, have stomach pain, swelling or breathing difficulty. Stop the medicine and get medical help.
entries.source: NHS - Ibuprofen for adults; MedlinePlus - Ibuprofen

entries.content: Antibiotics treat bacterial infections, not viruses such as colds and flu. They should only be taken when prescribed by a health worker. Taking them wrongly, sharing them or keeping leftovers contributes to antibiotic resistance, which makes infections harder to treat.
tips: Take exactly as prescribed for the full time you were told
Never share antibiotics or use leftovers
Do not ask for antibiotics for a cold or flu
entries.see_doctor_if: You develop a rash, swelling of the face or lips, or difficulty breathing. These may be signs of an allergic reaction and need emergency care.

entries.content: Oral rehydration salts (ORS) replace the water and salts the body loses during diarrhoea or vomiting. Mix the packet with clean, safe water exactly as the instructions say, and give small, frequent sips.
tips: Use clean, safe water and follow the packet instructions
Give small sips often, especially to children
Keep feeding and breastfeeding
entries.see_doctor_if: Diarrhoea lasts more than a few days, there is blood in the stool, the person cannot drink, or a baby or young child seems very unwell. Go to a health facility.

entries.content: Some symptoms need emergency care straight away: chest pain or pressure, difficulty breathing, sudden weakness or numbness, face drooping or slurred speech, severe bleeding, a seizure, loss of consciousness, a severe allergic reaction, or thoughts of harming yourself.
tips: Go to the nearest health facility or call your local emergency number
Do not drive yourself if you feel very unwell
Tell someone nearby so they can help
entries.see_doctor_if: Any of the signs above appear. Do not wait or rely on this app.
entries.source: WHO - Emergency care; NHS - When to call 999 or go to A&E

entries.content: Fever is often the body's response to an infection, and many fevers settle on their own. Some fevers need prompt medical care, especially in babies, in malaria areas, or when other warning signs are present.
tips: Drink plenty of fluids and rest
Dress lightly and keep the room comfortable
In a malaria area, get tested the same day
entries.see_doctor_if: A baby under 3 months has any fever, the fever lasts more than 3 days, or it comes with stiff neck, severe headache, rash, confusion, convulsions, difficulty breathing or constant vomiting.
entries.source: NHS - High temperature (fever) in adults; WHO - Malaria fact sheet

entries.content: Some symptoms should be checked even if you feel fairly well: a cough lasting 2 weeks or more, unexplained weight loss, night sweats, blood in urine, stool or cough, a lump that is growing, or a wound that does not heal.
tips: Note when the symptom started and whether it is changing
Visit a health facility for an assessment
Do not wait for it to become severe
entries.see_doctor_if: You have any of these symptoms. Make an appointment soon, and go urgently if they come with breathing difficulty or heavy bleeding.
entries.source: WHO - Tuberculosis fact sheet; NHS - Health A to Z

entries.content: A common cold is a mild viral infection of the nose and throat. Most people recover on their own within 1 to 2 weeks.
tips: Rest and drink plenty of fluids
Take paracetamol or ibuprofen as directed on the label for aches or fever
Wash your hands often and use a tissue when sneezing to avoid spreading it
entries.see_doctor_if: Symptoms last longer than 3 weeks, you have difficulty breathing or chest pain, or a baby or a person with a long-term illness is very unwell.

entries.condition: Viral infection with sudden fever and aches
entries.content: Flu is a viral infection that starts suddenly with fever, aching muscles and tiredness. Most healthy people recover within about a week.
tips: Rest, keep warm and drink plenty of fluids
Take paracetamol as directed to ease fever and aches
Stay at home while unwell so you do not spread it to others
entries.see_doctor_if: You have chest pain or difficulty breathing, symptoms are not improving after a week, or you are pregnant, elderly, a young child, or have a long-term condition.

entries.content: Most coughs are caused by infections such as colds and usually clear up by themselves within about 3 weeks.
tips: Drink warm drinks; honey and lemon can soothe a cough (do not give honey to babies under 1 year)
Stay hydrated and rest
Avoid smoke and other irritants
entries.see_doctor_if: Your cough lasts more than 2 to 3 weeks, you cough up blood, lose weight, have night sweats, or have chest pain or breathlessness. A cough lasting 2 weeks or more should be checked for TB.

entries.content: Most sore throats are caused by viruses and get better within about a week without antibiotics.
tips: Gargle with warm salty water (adults and older children)
Drink plenty of cool or warm fluids
Take paracetamol as directed to ease the pain
entries.see_doctor_if: You have difficulty swallowing or breathing, are drooling, have a very high temperature, or the sore throat lasts longer than a week.

entries.content: A fever is a body temperature of about 38 degrees C or above. It is a sign the body is fighting an infection. In malaria areas, any fever should be tested for malaria.
tips: Rest and drink plenty of fluids
Wear light clothing and keep the room cool
Take paracetamol as directed on the label
entries.see_doctor_if: A baby under 3 months has a fever, or the fever comes with a stiff neck, confusion, fits, a rash that does not fade when pressed, or lasts more than 3 days. In a malaria area, get tested the same day.

entries.content: Most headaches are tension-related and can be managed with rest, hydration, and over-the-counter pain relief.
tips: Drink water and rest in a quiet, dark room
Apply a cool cloth to your forehead
Take paracetamol or ibuprofen as directed
entries.see_doctor_if: You have a sudden, severe headache, or headache with vision changes, confusion, or stiff neck.

entries.content: Diarrhoea means passing loose, watery stools three or more times a day. The main danger is losing too much body fluid (dehydration), which can be prevented with oral rehydration solution (ORS).
tips: Drink plenty of fluids and use ORS to replace lost water and salts
Keep eating small, regular meals
Wash hands with soap after the toilet and before preparing food
entries.see_doctor_if: There is blood in the stool, diarrhoea lasts more than 7 days, you have a high fever, or you have signs of dehydration such as extreme thirst, dark urine, dizziness or very little urine.

entries.content: Vomiting is often caused by a stomach bug or food poisoning and usually settles within a day or two.
tips: Drink small, frequent sips of water or ORS
Rest and avoid solid food until the vomiting eases
Reintroduce small, plain meals when you feel able
entries.see_doctor_if: Vomiting lasts more than 2 days, there is blood in the vomit, severe stomach pain, severe headache with stiff neck, or signs of dehydration.

entries.content: Constipation means passing stools less often than usual, or stools that are hard and painful. It can usually be improved with diet and lifestyle changes.
tips: Eat more fibre such as fruit, vegetables, beans and whole grains
Drink plenty of water
Be physically active and go to the toilet when you feel the urge
entries.see_doctor_if: You have blood in your stool, severe stomach pain, unexplained weight loss, or constipation does not improve after about a week of these changes.

entries.condition: Burning feeling in the chest or upper stomach
entries.content: Heartburn and indigestion happen when stomach acid irritates the food pipe or stomach. Lifestyle changes often help.
tips: Eat smaller meals and avoid eating late at night
Limit fatty or spicy food, alcohol and caffeine
Do not smoke, and raise your head when sleeping
entries.see_doctor_if: You have difficulty swallowing, keep vomiting, have black stools, lose weight without trying, or have chest pain that could be heart-related.

entries.content: Most back pain improves within a few weeks. Staying active usually helps recovery more than bed rest.
tips: Keep moving and do gentle activity as pain allows
Use a warm or cold pack on the sore area
Take paracetamol as directed on the label
entries.see_doctor_if: You have numbness around the groin or buttocks, trouble controlling urine or stool, weakness in the legs, fever, pain after an injury, or pain that is not improving after a few weeks.

entries.condition: Pain in or around a tooth
entries.content: Toothache is usually caused by tooth decay or gum infection and needs a dentist or oral health worker to treat the cause.
tips: Rinse gently with warm salty water
Avoid very hot, cold or sugary food and drinks
Take paracetamol as directed and brush with fluoride toothpaste
entries.see_doctor_if: You have a swollen face or jaw, fever, or trouble swallowing or breathing (urgent), or tooth pain that lasts more than a day or two.

entries.content: Many rashes and itchy skin problems are mild, caused by irritation, allergy or minor infection, and settle with simple care.
tips: Avoid scratching and keep your skin cool
Stop using any new soap, cream or product that may be the cause
Keep skin moisturised with a plain, unperfumed moisturiser
entries.see_doctor_if: The rash comes with fever, spreads quickly, blisters, or does not fade when a glass is pressed against it. Swelling of the lips or face or difficulty breathing is an emergency.

entries.content: Earache is often caused by an ear infection and usually settles within a few days.
tips: Take paracetamol as directed to ease pain
Hold a warm cloth against the ear
Do not put anything inside the ear
entries.see_doctor_if: There is fluid or pus coming from the ear, hearing loss, swelling behind the ear, a high fever, or symptoms last more than 3 days.

entries.content: Conjunctivitis is a common eye infection or allergy that causes red, sticky or watery eyes. Infectious types often clear up within 1 to 2 weeks.
tips: Clean the eyelids with cooled boiled water and clean cotton wool
Wash your hands often and do not share towels
Avoid touching or rubbing the eyes
entries.see_doctor_if: You have severe eye pain, changes in vision, sensitivity to light, an eye injury, or a newborn baby has a red or sticky eye.

entries.content: Malaria is a life-threatening disease spread by the bites of infected female Anopheles mosquitoes. Early symptoms are fever, headache and chills, so getting tested early is important.
tips: Sleep under an insecticide-treated mosquito net every night
Get a malaria test as soon as you have a fever
Take the full course of treatment exactly as prescribed
entries.see_doctor_if: Go to a health facility the same day for any fever in a malaria area. Seek emergency care for extreme tiredness, confusion, repeated convulsions, difficulty breathing, dark or bloody urine, yellow skin or eyes, or abnormal bleeding. Children under 5 and pregnant women are at higher risk.

entries.condition: Bacterial infection mainly of the lungs
entries.content: TB is a bacterial infection that mostly affects the lungs and spreads through the air when a person with active TB coughs. It is curable with a full course of treatment.
tips: Cover your mouth when coughing and keep rooms well ventilated
Get tested if you have had a cough for 2 weeks or more
Take every dose of TB medicine until the course is finished
entries.see_doctor_if: You have a cough lasting 2 weeks or more, coughing up blood, fever, night sweats or weight loss. People living with HIV and close contacts of someone with TB should be checked.

entries.condition: Virus that weakens the immune system
entries.content: HIV is a virus that weakens the immune system. It spreads through unprotected sex, infected blood and from mother to child, not through everyday contact. With antiretroviral treatment (ART) people can live long, healthy lives.
tips: Get tested for HIV at a health facility
Use condoms correctly every time you have sex
If diagnosed, start ART and take it every day; pregnant women should be tested to protect their baby
entries.see_doctor_if: You think you may have been exposed. Go to a clinic as soon as possible, ideally within 72 hours, to ask about post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP). Also seek care for ongoing fever, weight loss or repeated infections.

entries.condition: Severe diarrhoeal infection from contaminated water
entries.content: Cholera is an infection caused by contaminated food or water. It can cause severe watery diarrhoea and kill within hours if not treated, but most cases can be treated with ORS.
tips: Drink only safe water (boiled or treated)
Wash hands with soap after the toilet and before eating or cooking
Start ORS immediately and go to a health facility
entries.see_doctor_if: You have profuse watery diarrhoea, repeated vomiting, leg cramps, extreme thirst or sunken eyes. This is an emergency, especially for children.

entries.condition: Bacterial infection from contaminated food or water
entries.content: Typhoid fever is a bacterial infection spread through contaminated food and water. It causes a fever that lasts for days, headache and stomach pain, and is treated with antibiotics.
tips: Drink safe water and eat food that is well cooked and freshly prepared
Wash hands with soap before eating and after using the toilet
Take antibiotics exactly as prescribed and get vaccinated where recommended
entries.see_doctor_if: You have a fever lasting several days with stomach pain, constipation or diarrhoea. Seek urgent care for confusion, severe abdominal pain or blood in the stool.

entries.content: Bilharzia is a parasitic disease caught from freshwater lakes, rivers and ponds containing infected snails. A common sign is blood in the urine or stool.
tips: Avoid swimming, washing or wading in water known to carry bilharzia
Take the treatment (praziquantel) when offered by the health service or school programme
Use safe water for bathing and washing
entries.see_doctor_if: You notice blood in your urine or stool, stomach pain, or ongoing symptoms after contact with freshwater in an area where bilharzia occurs.

entries.content: Pneumonia is an infection of the lungs and is a leading cause of death in children under 5. It causes cough, fever and fast or difficult breathing, and is treatable with antibiotics.
tips: Complete any antibiotics exactly as prescribed
Breastfeed babies exclusively for 6 months and keep children's vaccinations up to date
Keep cooking smoke and tobacco smoke away from children
entries.see_doctor_if: A child or adult has fast or difficult breathing, chest indrawing, bluish lips, cannot drink, or is very sleepy. This is an emergency.

entries.condition: Highly contagious viral illness with rash
entries.content: Measles is a highly contagious viral disease causing fever, rash, cough, runny nose and red eyes. It can be serious in young children and is prevented by vaccination.
tips: Vaccinate children on time with the measles vaccine
Keep the sick child at home and encourage fluids
Give vitamin A only as advised by a health worker
entries.see_doctor_if: A child has difficulty breathing, convulsions, ear discharge or signs of dehydration. Go to a health facility as soon as measles is suspected.

entries.condition: Respiratory illness caused by a coronavirus
entries.content: COVID-19 is a respiratory illness that ranges from mild to severe. Most people recover at home, but some groups are at higher risk of serious illness.
tips: Stay home and rest when unwell, and keep rooms ventilated
Wash hands often and wear a mask in crowded or enclosed places if you are unwell
Keep up to date with recommended vaccines
entries.see_doctor_if: You have difficulty breathing, persistent chest pain, confusion, bluish lips, or you are in a high-risk group and getting worse.

entries.content: Hepatitis B is a viral liver infection spread through blood, sexual contact and from mother to baby. It can be prevented with a safe and effective vaccine.
tips: Get vaccinated, and make sure babies receive their hepatitis B vaccine
Do not share needles, razors or toothbrushes
Use condoms and ask to be tested if you may have been exposed
entries.see_doctor_if: You have yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, severe tiredness, stomach pain or persistent vomiting. Pregnant women should be tested so the baby can be protected.

entries.content: High blood pressure often has no symptoms but raises the risk of heart attack, stroke and kidney disease. Regular checks and treatment can prevent complications.
tips: Have your blood pressure checked regularly
Eat less salt, be active, avoid tobacco and limit alcohol
Take prescribed medicine every day and do not stop it without advice
entries.see_doctor_if: You have a severe headache with confusion, chest pain, vision problems, or weakness or numbness on one side of the body. These are emergencies.

entries.condition: Long-term condition with high blood sugar
entries.content: Diabetes is a long-term condition where blood sugar stays too high. Common signs are increased thirst, frequent urination, tiredness, weight loss and slow-healing wounds.
tips: Eat a balanced diet and limit sugary drinks
Be physically active and check your feet regularly
Take medicines or insulin exactly as prescribed
entries.see_doctor_if: You have symptoms of diabetes and have not been tested. Seek emergency care for vomiting, drowsiness, confusion, fast breathing or a fruity smell on the breath.

entries.content: Asthma is a long-term lung condition that causes wheezing, coughing and breathlessness. It can be controlled with the right treatment and by avoiding triggers.
tips: Use your reliever and preventer inhalers as prescribed
Avoid triggers such as smoke, dust and strong smells
Follow a written asthma action plan from your health worker
entries.see_doctor_if: You are very breathless, cannot speak in full sentences, your reliever is not helping, or your lips turn blue. This is an emergency.

entries.condition: Low red blood cells or haemoglobin
entries.content: Anaemia means the blood carries too little oxygen. Common causes include iron deficiency, malaria and worm infections. It causes tiredness, pale skin and breathlessness.
tips: Eat iron-rich foods such as beans, green leafy vegetables, meat and fish, with fruit or vegetables rich in vitamin C
Take iron and folic acid supplements if given by a health worker, for example in pregnancy
Prevent and treat malaria and worm infections
entries.see_doctor_if: You feel persistently tired, look pale, or are dizzy or breathless. Seek urgent care for chest pain, fainting or severe breathlessness.

entries.content: Epilepsy is a condition that causes repeated seizures. Most people can control seizures with regular medicine. Knowing seizure first aid keeps the person safe.
tips: Stay with the person, time the seizure and cushion their head
Clear hard objects away and loosen tight clothing; never put anything in their mouth or hold them down
After the shaking stops, gently turn them onto their side
entries.see_doctor_if: It is a first seizure, lasts longer than 5 minutes, repeats without recovery, the person is injured, pregnant, or has trouble breathing afterwards. Call for emergency help.

entries.content: Most minor cuts and grazes can be treated at home by stopping the bleeding and keeping the wound clean.
tips: Wash your hands, then rinse the wound under clean running water
Press firmly with a clean cloth to stop the bleeding
Cover with a clean dressing and keep it clean and dry
entries.see_doctor_if: The wound is deep, will not stop bleeding after 10 minutes of pressure, has dirt in it, is an animal or human bite, or shows signs of infection such as spreading redness, pus or fever. Ask about tetanus protection.

entries.condition: Injury from heat, hot liquid or fire
entries.content: Cool a burn quickly to reduce damage and pain. Many small burns can be treated at home, but larger or deeper burns need medical care.
tips: Cool the burn under cool (not ice-cold) running water for 20 minutes
Remove jewellery and clothing near the burn unless stuck to the skin
Cover loosely with clean cling film or a clean non-fluffy cloth; do not apply ice, butter or toothpaste
entries.see_doctor_if: The burn is bigger than the person's hand, deep, blistered, or on the face, hands, feet or genitals. Also go for all chemical or electrical burns and all burns in young children.

entries.content: Most nosebleeds are not serious and stop within about 10 to 15 minutes if you apply pressure correctly.
tips: Sit up and lean forward; do not tip your head back
Pinch the soft part of the nose firmly for 10 to 15 minutes
Breathe through your mouth and spit out any blood
entries.see_doctor_if: The bleeding lasts more than 20 minutes, is heavy, follows a head injury, or you feel dizzy or weak.

entries.condition: Airway blocked by food or an object
entries.content: Choking happens when something blocks the airway. If the person can cough, encourage them. If they cannot speak, cough or breathe, act immediately. Babies and young children need a different technique, so learn first aid.
tips: Encourage the person to keep coughing
If they cannot cough, give up to 5 firm back blows between the shoulder blades
If that fails, give up to 5 abdominal thrusts (hands joined above the navel, pulling inwards and upwards)
entries.see_doctor_if: The object does not come out: call for emergency help straight away and keep repeating the steps. Anyone who received abdominal thrusts should be checked by a health worker.

entries.content: Sprains and strains usually get better with rest and simple care over a few days to weeks.
tips: Rest the injured part and avoid activities that cause pain
Apply an ice pack wrapped in a cloth for up to 20 minutes every few hours
Use gentle compression and keep the limb raised when resting
entries.see_doctor_if: You cannot put weight on the limb, have severe pain, numbness, an obvious deformity, or it is not improving after a few days.

entries.content: Fainting is a short loss of consciousness, often caused by a drop in blood flow to the brain. Most people recover quickly.
tips: Lay the person flat and raise their legs
Loosen tight clothing and make sure they have fresh air
When they recover, help them sit up slowly and give water
entries.see_doctor_if: They do not recover within a minute or two, are injured, have chest pain or palpitations, are pregnant, or this is the first time they have fainted.

entries.content: Snake bites can be life-threatening, but prompt care at a health facility saves lives. Antivenom is only given by health workers.
tips: Keep the person calm and still, and keep the bitten limb as still as possible
Remove rings and tight items near the bite
Get to a health facility quickly; do not cut, suck, tie a tight band or use traditional remedies on the bite
entries.see_doctor_if: All snake bites are emergencies. Get to a health facility immediately, especially if there is swelling, pain, bleeding, drowsiness or trouble breathing.

entries.content: Heat exhaustion causes heavy sweating, headache, dizziness and weakness. If it is not treated it can become heatstroke, which is an emergency.
tips: Move to a cool, shaded place and lie down
Remove extra clothing and sip cool water
Cool the skin with a wet cloth or fan
entries.see_doctor_if: The person is not improving after 30 minutes, has a very high temperature, confusion, fits or loses consciousness. These are signs of heatstroke and need emergency care.

entries.condition: Swallowing or contact with a harmful substance
entries.content: Poisoning can come from medicines, household chemicals, pesticides and some plants. Children are at particular risk. Quick action matters.
tips: Move the person away from the source and do not make them vomit
Keep the container or label to show the health worker
Store medicines, pesticides and paraffin out of children's reach
entries.see_doctor_if: Suspected poisoning is always an emergency. Go to the nearest health facility or call emergency services, especially if there is drowsiness, trouble breathing or fits.

entries.content: A broken bone causes pain, swelling and sometimes a visible deformity. It needs medical assessment and often an X-ray.
tips: Keep the injured part still and support it with padding or a sling
Do not try to straighten the limb
Apply an ice pack wrapped in cloth and control any bleeding with clean pressure
entries.see_doctor_if: You suspect a fracture. Seek urgent medical help, especially if there is an open wound, severe pain, deformity, numbness or a blue or pale limb.

entries.content: High blood pressure is diagnosed when readings taken at rest are raised on at least 3 separate occasions. It usually causes no symptoms, so it is found by measuring. In adults, a reading of 140/90 mmHg or more is high.
tips: Reduce the amount of salt in your food
Do regular exercise
Lose weight if you are overweight
entries.see_doctor_if: Your blood pressure is high on checks. All children with high blood pressure should be seen by a doctor. Seek urgent care for severe headache, confusion or fits.

entries.content: Heart failure means the heart cannot pump blood well. Signs include shortness of breath, cough, tiredness, difficulty exercising, breathlessness when lying flat or waking at night, and swelling. Causes include high blood pressure, rheumatic heart disease and heart muscle disease.
tips: Cut down on salt and follow advice about how much fluid to drink
Stop smoking and alcohol
Take moderate exercise and weigh yourself daily as advised
entries.see_doctor_if: You have new or worsening breathlessness, swelling of the legs, or unusual tiredness. Heart failure needs a proper check to find the cause.
entries.source: MSTG 2023 (6th ed.) - Section 2.2 Congestive heart failure

entries.condition: Sudden chest pain from reduced blood flow to the heart
entries.content: A heart attack causes sudden chest pain that feels like tightness or heaviness, often lasting more than 30 minutes and not eased by rest. The pain may spread to the left arm, neck or jaw, with sweating, nausea and breathlessness. In people with diabetes and older adults, breathlessness or tiredness may be the only sign.
tips: Stop what you are doing and rest while help is arranged
Get to a hospital immediately
Control risk factors: high blood pressure, diabetes, smoking, obesity and high cholesterol
entries.see_doctor_if: Anyone with sudden severe chest pain, sweating, breathlessness or fainting should go to hospital immediately. This is an emergency.
entries.source: MSTG 2023 (6th ed.) - Section 2.9 Acute coronary syndrome

entries.content: A stroke happens when blood supply to part of the brain is blocked or a blood vessel bleeds. Signs include weakness or paralysis on one side, drooping of the face, confusion, difficulty speaking, vision problems and fits. High blood pressure, sickle cell disease and some infections can cause stroke.
tips: Get to a hospital immediately
Do not give food or drink until swallowing has been checked by a health worker
Have blood pressure and blood sugar checked
entries.see_doctor_if: Any sudden weakness on one side, facial droop, confusion or trouble speaking is an emergency.

entries.content: A seizure is a burst of abnormal electrical activity in the brain. Causes include fever with infections such as malaria (febrile convulsions in children aged 6 months to 6 years), cerebral malaria, meningitis, low blood sugar, head injury, poisoning and epilepsy.
tips: Keep the person safe, away from hard objects, and lying on their side
Do not put anything in the mouth
Take them to a health facility so the cause can be found, including a blood sugar check
entries.see_doctor_if: It is a first fit, a fit with fever, a fit that does not stop, or a fit in a baby or pregnant woman. Go to a health facility.
entries.source: MSTG 2023 (6th ed.) - Section 3.1 Seizures and epilepsy

entries.content: Migraine is a repeated headache, often on one side, that may come with warning signs (aura), nausea and vomiting. It is not dangerous in itself, and finding and avoiding triggers can help.
tips: Start treatment at the first sign of an attack
Try to identify triggers and reduce tension
Reassurance helps: migraine is a harmless condition
entries.see_doctor_if: You have weakness or numbness, a sudden very severe headache, or migraines that do not respond to treatment. These need further checks, including a brain scan.

entries.condition: Infection of the covering of the brain
entries.content: Meningitis is an infection of the membranes covering the brain. The typical signs are headache, stiff neck and fever, often with vomiting and dislike of light. A blotchy red rash can occur with one type.
tips: Go to hospital immediately; do not wait
Tell the health worker about any rash or confusion
Early treatment saves lives
entries.see_doctor_if: Anyone with headache, stiff neck and fever, a drowsy or confused person, or a child with a rash and fever. This is an emergency.

entries.condition: Ear pain, discharge or swelling behind the ear
entries.content: Mastoiditis is an infection that spreads to the bone behind the ear, usually from untreated middle ear infection. Signs are swelling behind or above the ear, ear discharge, fever and an ear pushed forward.
tips: Seek medical care as soon as ear symptoms start
Eat food rich in vitamins such as fruit and vegetables
Avoid spicy food
entries.see_doctor_if: There is swelling behind the ear, ear discharge or fever. Go to a health facility; it can spread to the brain if untreated.

entries.content: Nosebleeds are common and are caused by injury, nose picking, infections, high blood pressure, bleeding disorders and anaemia.
tips: Lean forward and pinch the nose for 5 to 10 minutes
Breathe through the mouth
A cold pack on the forehead may help
entries.see_doctor_if: The bleeding does not stop, it keeps coming back, or you also have other bleeding or very high blood pressure. A health worker can treat the bleeding point.

entries.content: Tonsillitis causes a sore throat, painful swallowing, red tonsils with white spots and sudden fever. It is often caused by streptococcal bacteria and sometimes needs antibiotics from a health worker.
tips: Gargle with warm salt water
Use pain relief as advised by a health worker
Drink fluids
entries.see_doctor_if: You have a sore throat with fever and white spots, a swollen throat abscess, or 4 to 5 attacks in a year. Ask about referral.

entries.content: The common cold is a viral infection that usually clears within a week. Signs include runny or blocked nose, sneezing, cough, sore throat, mild headache and low fever. Young children can have fever for up to 72 hours. In babies, a blocked nose can make feeding difficult.
tips: Rest and drink plenty of fluids
Gargle lukewarm salt water
Do not use cough syrups for children with respiratory infections
entries.see_doctor_if: A child is breathing fast or with difficulty, cannot drink, or is getting worse. Also see a health worker for ear pain or a painful throat that develops.

entries.content: Pneumonia in a child shows as cough with fast breathing or the chest pulling in. It becomes severe if the child cannot drink, vomits everything, has fits, is very sleepy or unconscious, or is severely malnourished.
tips: Keep feeding and giving fluids during the illness
Watch closely for danger signs
Do not use cough syrups
entries.see_doctor_if: A child has difficulty breathing, fast breathing, cannot drink, or is getting worse. Take them to a health facility immediately.
entries.source: MSTG 2023 (6th ed.) - Sections 16.1.1 and 16.2.6 Respiratory infections in children

entries.content: Asthma is a long-term airway condition causing recurring wheeze, cough, chest tightness and breathlessness. Triggers include dust mites, smoke, fumes, perfumes, pollen, infections, pet hair, cold weather, exercise, strong emotions, some foods and some medicines such as aspirin.
tips: Identify and avoid your triggers
Keep taking prescribed treatment and attend follow-up
Avoid smoke and strong smells
entries.see_doctor_if: You have a severe attack, cannot speak in full sentences, or your usual treatment is not working. Go to a health facility immediately.

entries.content: COPD is a long-term lung disease with breathlessness, cough and sputum that does not fully reverse. In Malawi the main risk factor is smoke from cooking indoors with firewood, charcoal or other solid fuels. Smoking and past lung damage such as TB also cause it.
tips: Cook in a well-ventilated space and reduce smoke at home
Do not smoke
Attend follow-up and treat chest infections early
entries.see_doctor_if: Your breathlessness is getting worse, you cough up a lot of sputum, or your lips turn blue. Seek care promptly.
entries.source: MSTG 2023 (6th ed.) - Section 16.2.16 Chronic lung disease / COPD

entries.content: Anaemia means the blood carries too little oxygen. Common causes include iron deficiency, malaria and worm infections. It causes tiredness, pale skin and breathlessness.
tips: Eat iron-rich foods such as beans, green leafy vegetables, meat and fish, with fruit or vegetables rich in vitamin C
Take iron and folic acid supplements if given by a health worker, for example in pregnancy
Prevent and treat malaria and worm infections
entries.see_doctor_if: You feel persistently tired, look pale, or are dizzy or breathless. Seek urgent care for chest pain, fainting or severe breathlessness.

entries.condition: Long-term condition with high blood sugar
entries.content: Diabetes is a long-term condition where blood sugar stays too high. Common signs are increased thirst, frequent urination, tiredness, weight loss and slow-healing wounds.
tips: Eat a balanced diet and limit sugary drinks
Be physically active and check your feet regularly
Take medicines or insulin exactly as prescribed
entries.see_doctor_if: You have symptoms of diabetes and have not been tested. Seek emergency care for vomiting, drowsiness, confusion, fast breathing or a fruity smell on the breath.

entries.condition: Watery stools for less than 14 days
entries.content: Acute diarrhoea is three or more watery stools a day lasting less than 14 days. The danger is dehydration.
tips: Drink plenty of water and use a sugar and salt solution (ORS) to replace lost salts, especially for children
Wash hands regularly and avoid spoiled or contaminated food
Eat freshly heated food and drink boiled or chlorine-treated water
entries.see_doctor_if: You pass loose stools more than three times a day, there is blood in the stool, or you cannot keep fluids down. Go to a health facility.

entries.condition: Loose stools for more than 4 weeks
entries.content: Chronic diarrhoea means loose stools more than 3 times a day for over 4 weeks. It is common in people with HIV and needs a cause to be found.
tips: Drink oral rehydration solution to replace fluids
Get an HIV test if you have not had one
Follow the hygiene advice for diarrhoea
entries.see_doctor_if: Diarrhoea lasts more than 4 weeks, or you are losing weight or feeling weak. See a health worker.

entries.content: Ulcers and gastritis are often caused by the bacterium Helicobacter pylori. Signs include burning stomach pain, often worse when empty or at night. Pain-killers such as aspirin and ibuprofen (NSAIDs), alcohol and smoking raise the risk.
tips: Avoid spicy food, alcohol, tobacco and fizzy drinks
Avoid foods that make the pain worse
Do not take aspirin or ibuprofen if you have had an ulcer
entries.see_doctor_if: You vomit blood, pass black stools, lose weight, have trouble swallowing, are anaemic, or have ongoing pain. See a health worker.
entries.source: MSTG 2023 (6th ed.) - Section 7.6 Peptic ulcer disease / gastritis

entries.content: Hepatitis B is the most common type of long-term viral hepatitis. It can pass from mother to child at birth or spread through blood. A person has chronic infection if the surface antigen stays positive for 6 months or more. It may cause no symptoms, or serious liver damage such as swelling of the belly or vomiting blood.
tips: Pregnant women should be tested for hepatitis B at their first antenatal visit
Get tested, and ask whether you are eligible for treatment
Protect others: do not share razors, needles or other items with blood on them
entries.see_doctor_if: You have a positive test, yellow eyes, a swollen belly, vomiting blood or confusion. See a health worker promptly.
entries.source: MSTG 2023 (6th ed.) - Section 8.1 Chronic viral hepatitis; Section 9.1.1

entries.condition: Virus that weakens the immune system
entries.content: HIV is a virus that weakens the immune system. It spreads through unprotected sex, infected blood and from mother to child, not through everyday contact. With antiretroviral treatment (ART) people can live long, healthy lives.
tips: Get tested for HIV at a health facility
Use condoms correctly every time you have sex
If diagnosed, start ART and take it every day; pregnant women should be tested to protect their baby
entries.see_doctor_if: You think you may have been exposed. Go to a clinic as soon as possible, ideally within 72 hours, to ask about post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP). Also seek care for ongoing fever, weight loss or repeated infections.

entries.condition: Bacterial infection mainly of the lungs
entries.content: TB is a bacterial infection that mostly affects the lungs and spreads through the air when a person with active TB coughs. It is curable with a full course of treatment.
tips: Cover your mouth when coughing and keep rooms well ventilated
Get tested if you have had a cough for 2 weeks or more
Take every dose of TB medicine until the course is finished
entries.see_doctor_if: You have a cough lasting 2 weeks or more, coughing up blood, fever, night sweats or weight loss. People living with HIV and close contacts of someone with TB should be checked.

entries.condition: Severe watery diarrhoea from contaminated water
entries.content: Cholera is a bacterial infection that causes severe, usually painless, rice-water diarrhoea with vomiting. It can kill within hours. Replacing fluids is the main treatment.
tips: Start oral rehydration solution immediately and go to a health facility
Isolate the sick person and wash hands carefully after contact
Report suspected cases to the health authorities
entries.see_doctor_if: Anyone with sudden severe watery diarrhoea and vomiting should be taken to a health facility immediately, especially children.

entries.content: Bacillary dysentery (shigellosis) causes bloody, mucus-filled diarrhoea with abdominal pain. Antibiotics are used only for people who are very unwell, septic or have weak immunity.
tips: Wash hands with soap
Practise food hygiene and dispose of faeces safely
Isolate the patient and use hygiene precautions around them
entries.see_doctor_if: There is blood in the stool. Go to a health facility, especially for a child, an older person, or someone with a high fever.

entries.content: Constipation means passing stools less often than usual, or stools that are hard and painful. It is often related to too little fibre. It is important to look for a cause if it continues.
tips: Eat a high-fibre diet such as vegetables and fruit; papaya seeds are mentioned in the guidelines
Drink more fluids
Do not give oral laxatives to children
entries.see_doctor_if: A newborn has not passed stool in the first 48 hours (especially with vomiting or a swollen belly), an infant is constipated, or constipation is long-lasting despite fibre and fluids.

entries.content: Ulcers and gastritis are often caused by the bacterium Helicobacter pylori. Signs include burning stomach pain, often worse when empty or at night. Pain-killers such as aspirin and ibuprofen (NSAIDs), alcohol and smoking raise the risk.
tips: Avoid spicy food, alcohol, tobacco and fizzy drinks
Avoid foods that make the pain worse
Do not take aspirin or ibuprofen if you have had an ulcer
entries.see_doctor_if: You vomit blood, pass black stools, lose weight, have trouble swallowing, are anaemic, or have ongoing pain. See a health worker.
entries.source: MSTG 2023 (6th ed.) - Section 7.6 Peptic ulcer disease / gastritis

entries.content: Hepatitis B is the most common type of long-term viral hepatitis. It can pass from mother to child at birth or spread through blood. A person has chronic infection if the surface antigen stays positive for 6 months or more. It may cause no symptoms, or serious liver damage such as swelling of the belly or vomiting blood.
tips: Pregnant women should be tested for hepatitis B at their first antenatal visit
Get tested, and ask whether you are eligible for treatment
Protect others: do not share razors, needles or other items with blood on them
entries.see_doctor_if: You have a positive test, yellow eyes, a swollen belly, vomiting blood or confusion. See a health worker promptly.
entries.source: MSTG 2023 (6th ed.) - Section 8.1 Chronic viral hepatitis; Section 9.1.1

entries.condition: Virus that weakens the immune system
entries.content: HIV is a virus that weakens the immune system. It spreads through unprotected sex, infected blood and from mother to child, not through everyday contact. With antiretroviral treatment (ART) people can live long, healthy lives.
tips: Get tested for HIV at a health facility
Use condoms correctly every time you have sex
If diagnosed, start ART and take it every day; pregnant women should be tested to protect their baby
entries.see_doctor_if: You think you may have been exposed. Go to a clinic as soon as possible, ideally within 72 hours, to ask about post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP). Also seek care for ongoing fever, weight loss or repeated infections.

entries.condition: Bacterial infection mainly of the lungs
entries.content: TB is a bacterial infection that mostly affects the lungs and spreads through the air when a person with active TB coughs. It is curable with a full course of treatment.
tips: Cover your mouth when coughing and keep rooms well ventilated
Get tested if you have had a cough for 2 weeks or more
Take every dose of TB medicine until the course is finished
entries.see_doctor_if: You have a cough lasting 2 weeks or more, coughing up blood, fever, night sweats or weight loss. People living with HIV and close contacts of someone with TB should be checked.

entries.condition: Severe watery diarrhoea from contaminated water
entries.content: Cholera is a bacterial infection that causes severe, usually painless, rice-water diarrhoea with vomiting. It can kill within hours. Replacing fluids is the main treatment.
tips: Start oral rehydration solution immediately and go to a health facility
Isolate the sick person and wash hands carefully after contact
Report suspected cases to the health authorities
entries.see_doctor_if: Anyone with sudden severe watery diarrhoea and vomiting should be taken to a health facility immediately, especially children.

entries.condition: Bacterial infection from contaminated food or water
entries.content: Typhoid fever is a bacterial infection spread through contaminated food and water. It causes a fever that lasts for days, headache and stomach pain, and is treated with antibiotics.
tips: Drink safe water and eat food that is well cooked and freshly prepared
Wash hands with soap before eating and after using the toilet
Take antibiotics exactly as prescribed and get vaccinated where recommended
entries.see_doctor_if: You have a fever lasting several days with stomach pain, constipation or diarrhoea. Seek urgent care for confusion, severe abdominal pain or blood in the stool.

entries.content: Bilharzia is a parasitic disease caught from freshwater lakes, rivers and ponds containing infected snails. A common sign is blood in the urine or stool.
tips: Avoid swimming, washing or wading in water known to carry bilharzia
Take the treatment (praziquantel) when offered by the health service or school programme
Use safe water for bathing and washing
entries.see_doctor_if: You notice blood in your urine or stool, stomach pain, or ongoing symptoms after contact with freshwater in an area where bilharzia occurs.

entries.content: Pneumonia is an infection of the lungs and is a leading cause of death in children under 5. It causes cough, fever and fast or difficult breathing, and is treatable with antibiotics.
tips: Complete any antibiotics exactly as prescribed
Breastfeed babies exclusively for 6 months and keep children's vaccinations up to date
Keep cooking smoke and tobacco smoke away from children
entries.see_doctor_if: A child or adult has fast or difficult breathing, chest indrawing, bluish lips, cannot drink, or is very sleepy. This is an emergency.

entries.condition: Highly contagious viral illness with rash
entries.content: Measles is a highly contagious viral disease causing fever, rash, cough, runny nose and red eyes. It can be serious in young children and is prevented by vaccination.
tips: Vaccinate children on time with the measles vaccine
Keep the sick child at home and encourage fluids
Give vitamin A only as advised by a health worker
entries.see_doctor_if: A child has difficulty breathing, convulsions, ear discharge or signs of dehydration. Go to a health facility as soon as measles is suspected.

entries.condition: Respiratory illness caused by a coronavirus
entries.content: COVID-19 is a respiratory illness that ranges from mild to severe. Most people recover at home, but some groups are at higher risk of serious illness.
tips: Stay home and rest when unwell, and keep rooms ventilated
Wash hands often and wear a mask in crowded or enclosed places if you are unwell
Keep up to date with recommended vaccines
entries.see_doctor_if: You have difficulty breathing, persistent chest pain, confusion, bluish lips, or you are in a high-risk group and getting worse.

entries.content: Hepatitis B is a viral liver infection spread through blood, sexual contact and from mother to baby. It can be prevented with a safe and effective vaccine.
tips: Get vaccinated, and make sure babies receive their hepatitis B vaccine
Do not share needles, razors or toothbrushes
Use condoms and ask to be tested if you may have been exposed
entries.see_doctor_if: You have yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, severe tiredness, stomach pain or persistent vomiting. Pregnant women should be tested so the baby can be protected.

entries.content: High blood pressure often has no symptoms but raises the risk of heart attack, stroke and kidney disease. Regular checks and treatment can prevent complications.
tips: Have your blood pressure checked regularly
Eat less salt, be active, avoid tobacco and limit alcohol
Take prescribed medicine every day and do not stop it without advice
entries.see_doctor_if: You have a severe headache with confusion, chest pain, vision problems, or weakness or numbness on one side of the body. These are emergencies.

entries.condition: Long-term condition with high blood sugar
entries.content: Diabetes is a long-term condition where blood sugar stays too high. Common signs are increased thirst, frequent urination, tiredness, weight loss and slow-healing wounds.
tips: Eat a balanced diet and limit sugary drinks
Be physically active and check your feet regularly
Take medicines or insulin exactly as prescribed
entries.see_doctor_if: You have symptoms of diabetes and have not been tested. Seek emergency care for vomiting, drowsiness, confusion, fast breathing or a fruity smell on the breath.

entries.content: Asthma is a long-term lung condition that causes wheezing, coughing and breathlessness. It can be controlled with the right treatment and by avoiding triggers.
tips: Use your reliever and preventer inhalers as prescribed
Avoid triggers such as smoke, dust and strong smells
Follow a written asthma action plan from your health worker
entries.see_doctor_if: You are very breathless, cannot speak in full sentences, your reliever is not helping, or your lips turn blue. This is an emergency.

entries.condition: Low red blood cells or haemoglobin
entries.content: Anaemia means the blood carries too little oxygen. Common causes include iron deficiency, malaria and worm infections. It causes tiredness, pale skin and breathlessness.
tips: Eat iron-rich foods such as beans, green leafy vegetables, meat and fish, with fruit or vegetables rich in vitamin C
Take iron and folic acid supplements if given by a health worker, for example in pregnancy
Prevent and treat malaria and worm infections
entries.see_doctor_if: You feel persistently tired, look pale, or are dizzy or breathless. Seek urgent care for chest pain, fainting or severe breathlessness.

entries.content: Epilepsy is a condition that causes repeated seizures. Most people can control seizures with regular medicine. Knowing seizure first aid keeps the person safe.
tips: Stay with the person, time the seizure and cushion their head
Clear hard objects away and loosen tight clothing; never put anything in their mouth or hold them down
After the shaking stops, gently turn them onto their side
entries.see_doctor_if: It is a first seizure, lasts longer than 5 minutes, repeats without recovery, the person is injured, pregnant, or has trouble breathing afterwards. Call for emergency help.

entries.content: Most minor cuts and grazes can be treated at home by stopping the bleeding and keeping the wound clean.
tips: Wash your hands, then rinse the wound under clean running water
Press firmly with a clean cloth to stop the bleeding
Cover with a clean dressing and keep it clean and dry
entries.see_doctor_if: The wound is deep, will not stop bleeding after 10 minutes of pressure, has dirt in it, is an animal or human bite, or shows signs of infection such as spreading redness, pus or fever. Ask about tetanus protection.

entries.condition: Injury from heat, hot liquid or fire
entries.content: Cool a burn quickly to reduce damage and pain. Many small burns can be treated at home, but larger or deeper burns need medical care.
tips: Cool the burn under cool (not ice-cold) running water for 20 minutes
Remove jewellery and clothing near the burn unless stuck to the skin
Cover loosely with clean cling film or a clean non-fluffy cloth; do not apply ice, butter or toothpaste
entries.see_doctor_if: The burn is bigger than the person's hand, deep, blistered, or on the face, hands, feet or genitals. Also go for all chemical or electrical burns and all burns in young children.

entries.content: Most nosebleeds are not serious and stop within about 10 to 15 minutes if you apply pressure correctly.
tips: Sit up and lean forward; do not tip your head back
Pinch the soft part of the nose firmly for 10 to 15 minutes
Breathe through your mouth and spit out any blood
entries.see_doctor_if: The bleeding lasts more than 20 minutes, is heavy, follows a head injury, or you feel dizzy or weak.

entries.condition: Airway blocked by food or an object
entries.content: Choking happens when something blocks the airway. If the person can cough, encourage them. If they cannot speak, cough or breathe, act immediately. Babies and young children need a different technique, so learn first aid.
tips: Encourage the person to keep coughing
If they cannot cough, give up to 5 firm back blows between the shoulder blades
If that fails, give up to 5 abdominal thrusts (hands joined above the navel, pulling inwards and upwards)
entries.see_doctor_if: The object does not come out: call for emergency help straight away and keep repeating the steps. Anyone who received abdominal thrusts should be checked by a health worker.

entries.content: Sprains and strains usually get better with rest and simple care over a few days to weeks.
tips: Rest the injured part and avoid activities that cause pain
Apply an ice pack wrapped in a cloth for up to 20 minutes every few hours
Use gentle compression and keep the limb raised when resting
entries.see_doctor_if: You cannot put weight on the limb, have severe pain, numbness, an obvious deformity, or it is not improving after a few days.

entries.content: Fainting is a short loss of consciousness, often caused by a drop in blood flow to the brain. Most people recover quickly.
tips: Lay the person flat and raise their legs
Loosen tight clothing and make sure they have fresh air
When they recover, help them sit up slowly and give water
entries.see_doctor_if: They do not recover within a minute or two, are injured, have chest pain or palpitations, are pregnant, or this is the first time they have fainted.

entries.content: Snake bites can be life-threatening, but prompt care at a health facility saves lives. Antivenom is only given by health workers.
tips: Keep the person calm and still, and keep the bitten limb as still as possible
Remove rings and tight items near the bite
Get to a health facility quickly; do not cut, suck, tie a tight band or use traditional remedies on the bite
entries.see_doctor_if: All snake bites are emergencies. Get to a health facility immediately, especially if there is swelling, pain, bleeding, drowsiness or trouble breathing.

entries.content: Heat exhaustion causes heavy sweating, headache, dizziness and weakness. If it is not treated it can become heatstroke, which is an emergency.
tips: Move to a cool, shaded place and lie down
Remove extra clothing and sip cool water
Cool the skin with a wet cloth or fan
entries.see_doctor_if: The person is not improving after 30 minutes, has a very high temperature, confusion, fits or loses consciousness. These are signs of heatstroke and need emergency care.

entries.condition: Swallowing or contact with a harmful substance
entries.content: Poisoning can come from medicines, household chemicals, pesticides and some plants. Children are at particular risk. Quick action matters.
tips: Move the person away from the source and do not make them vomit
Keep the container or label to show the health worker
Store medicines, pesticides and paraffin out of children's reach
entries.see_doctor_if: Suspected poisoning is always an emergency. Go to the nearest health facility or call emergency services, especially if there is drowsiness, trouble breathing or fits.

entries.content: A broken bone causes pain, swelling and sometimes a visible deformity. It needs medical assessment and often an X-ray.
tips: Keep the injured part still and support it with padding or a sling
Do not try to straighten the limb
Apply an ice pack wrapped in cloth and control any bleeding with clean pressure
entries.see_doctor_if: You suspect a fracture. Seek urgent medical help, especially if there is an open wound, severe pain, deformity, numbness or a blue or pale limb.

entries.content: Regular antenatal care helps keep mother and baby healthy. Some symptoms during pregnancy can signal a serious problem and need urgent care.
tips: Attend all antenatal visits and plan to deliver at a health facility with a skilled attendant
Take iron and folic acid as advised and sleep under an insecticide-treated net
Eat a varied diet and avoid alcohol and tobacco
entries.see_doctor_if: Go immediately for vaginal bleeding, severe headache, blurred vision, swelling of face or hands, fits, high fever, severe abdominal pain, difficulty breathing, leaking fluid, or reduced or absent baby movements.

entries.condition: Feeding a baby with breast milk
entries.content: Breast milk is the ideal food for babies. WHO advises starting within the first hour after birth, exclusive breastfeeding for the first 6 months, then continuing with safe complementary foods up to 2 years or beyond.
tips: Start breastfeeding within the first hour after birth
Feed on demand, day and night, and check the baby has a good latch
From 6 months add safe, nutritious foods while continuing to breastfeed
entries.see_doctor_if: The baby is not feeding well, has fewer wet nappies, is gaining weight poorly, or the mother has breast pain with a red lump or fever. Mothers living with HIV should follow their health worker's advice.
entries.source: WHO - Infant and young child feeding

entries.content: Routine childhood vaccines protect against serious diseases such as measles, polio, tuberculosis, pneumonia, whooping cough, tetanus and hepatitis B.
tips: Follow the national immunisation schedule and keep the child's health card safe
Vaccinate on time; a mild illness is usually not a reason to delay
A mild fever or sore arm after a vaccine is common and usually passes quickly
entries.see_doctor_if: A child has missed vaccines. Ask a health worker about catching up.

entries.condition: Loss of too much body fluid
entries.content: Children lose fluid quickly with diarrhoea and vomiting. ORS and continued feeding prevent dehydration, and zinc given as advised by a health worker shortens diarrhoea.
tips: Give ORS in small, frequent sips and breastfeed more often
Keep feeding the child normally
Give zinc only as advised by a health worker
entries.see_doctor_if: The child has sunken eyes, no tears, a dry mouth, little or no urine, is drowsy or floppy, cannot drink, or has blood in the stool. Go to a health facility immediately.

entries.condition: Caring for a baby in the first weeks
entries.content: The first 28 days are the most vulnerable time in a child's life. Warmth, clean care and early breastfeeding keep newborns healthy.
tips: Keep the baby warm with skin-to-skin contact
Keep the cord stump clean and dry
Breastfeed early and often and wash hands before touching the baby
entries.see_doctor_if: The baby is not feeding, has a fever or feels very cold, breathes fast, has yellow skin or eyes, a red or pus-filled cord, fits, or is floppy. Seek care urgently.

entries.content: A healthy diet includes a variety of foods: vegetables, fruits, legumes, nuts and whole grains, and limits salt, sugar and unhealthy fats.
tips: Eat a variety of foods including at least 5 portions of fruit and vegetables a day
Eat less salt and sugar and choose water over sugary drinks
Choose cooking methods that use less oil and avoid too many fried foods
entries.see_doctor_if: You are losing weight without trying, have a long-term loss of appetite, or struggle to get enough food. Talk to a health worker or nutrition service.

entries.condition: Not enough food or nutrients for growth
entries.content: Malnutrition can show as being very thin, short for age, or swelling of the feet. Good feeding, growth checks and treating infections quickly protect children.
tips: Breastfeed exclusively for 6 months, then add a variety of foods such as beans, groundnuts, eggs, fish, fruit and vegetables
Attend growth monitoring at the clinic
Treat infections such as diarrhoea and malaria promptly
entries.see_doctor_if: A child is very thin, has swollen feet, a poor appetite, or is weak and sleepy. Take them to a health facility, where special therapeutic food may be given.

entries.content: Washing hands with soap and clean water is one of the most effective ways to prevent diarrhoea, respiratory infections and many other illnesses.
tips: Wet hands, apply soap and scrub all surfaces for at least 20 seconds
Wash before eating or preparing food and after using the toilet or changing a nappy
Wash after caring for someone who is sick
entries.see_doctor_if: Handwashing does not treat illness. See a health worker if you or a child has ongoing diarrhoea, fever or a skin infection.

entries.content: Unsafe water spreads diseases such as cholera, typhoid and diarrhoea. Boiling or treating water makes it safer to drink.
tips: Bring water to a rolling boil for at least 1 minute, or treat it with chlorine as instructed
Store treated water in a clean, covered container
Use a clean cup or ladle to take water out
entries.see_doctor_if: You or a child develop diarrhoea, vomiting or signs of dehydration after drinking untreated water.

entries.content: Stress and anxiety are common. Simple habits can help, and support is available when worry starts to affect daily life.
tips: Talk to someone you trust about how you are feeling
Get regular physical activity and enough sleep
Try slow, deep breathing and limit alcohol
entries.see_doctor_if: Worry is constant and affects daily life, you have panic attacks or weeks of poor sleep, or you use alcohol or drugs to cope. If you have thoughts of harming yourself, seek help right away from a health worker, emergency services or someone nearby.
entries.source: NHS - Stress, anxiety and low mood

entries.content: Depression means low mood, low energy and loss of enjoyment on most days for at least 2 weeks. Other signs are poor sleep or appetite, poor concentration, guilt or worthlessness. Illnesses such as anaemia, thyroid problems, HIV and syphilis can look like depression, so a health check is needed.
tips: Talk to a health worker or someone you trust
Stay connected with family and friends
Keep a routine of sleep, food and activity
entries.see_doctor_if: You have felt low for 2 weeks or more or find daily tasks hard. If you have thoughts of ending your life, tell someone now and go to a health facility or call emergency services.
entries.source: NHS - Stress, anxiety and low mood

entries.content: Alcohol can cause slurred speech, poor judgement and unsteady walking. Stopping suddenly after heavy drinking can cause withdrawal, usually 12 to 18 hours after the last drink and worst at 24 to 48 hours. Screening and brief advice on safe levels can help.
tips: Know and keep to safe levels of alcohol
Do not stop suddenly after heavy drinking without medical advice
Ask a health worker for screening
entries.see_doctor_if: You drink heavily and want to stop, or you shake, sweat or see things after stopping. Seek medical help.
